newsitem.title: CZECH REPUBLIC: Czech government faces vital confidence vote.
newsitem.headline: Czech government faces vital confidence vote.

text.p: The Czech government faces a knife-edge confidence vote in parliament this week which will determine the future of embattled Prime Minister Vaclav Klaus and his economic programme.

Klaus's three-party, centre-right coalition controls only 100 seats in the 200-seat lower house and even members of the government have been driving hard bargains for their support in the vote, which could come as early as Tuesday.
"The only thing we can say for certain is that it is going to be very close," said political analyst Jiri Pehe. "But I think it is likely at this point that the government will win," he added.

Coalition leaders met early on Monday and the full government was scheduled to meet later to hammer out a series of budget cuts that form part of an austerity programme one party wants adopted in exchange for its support.

"We discussed the willingness of our three political parties to talk about cutting state expenditure at a session of the government this afternoon," Klaus told reportrers after the coalition leaders' meeting.
Deputy Prime Minister Josef Lux's Christian Democratic Union (KDU-CSL) has said it wants the programme, agreed by coalition leaders late last month, adopted by the government.
"If he gets it (adopted), at least partly, it would be very difficult for him to bring down his own government," Pehe said.
The Christian Democrats also want measures to deregulate rents and energy prices, agreed in March, postponed.
The KDU-CSL and Michal Zantovsky's Civic Democratic Alliance (ODA) are insisting on a balanced budget but Klaus said the differences were not insurmountable.
In a clear reference to the KDU-CSL, Klaus warned waverers over the weekend that failure to support the government would be a leap into the unknown.

"If anyone wants to let the government fall, of course he has the right and the strength to do so, but I would ask him not to take a leap into the dark, not to leap into the unknown, to know what comes next," he said in a television discussion.
Klaus called the confidence vote last week after two weeks of turbulence in the foreign exchange markets.
Speculators, alarmed at widening current account and trade deficits and growing political uncertainty, short-sold the crown, leading the central bank to float the currency on May 27.
Coalition leaders the next day agreed a sweeping cabinet reshuffle and the austerity programme, which called for budget cuts totalling some 20 billion crowns and wage freezes.
The crown strengthened slightly against the dollar and mark on Monday on signs the government would win the vote and on positive economic data, traders said.
"The feeling now is that the government will win the confidence vote," said Tomas Becvar, a dealer Komercni Banka.
If Klaus lost the vote, he would be obliged under the constitution to step down, Pehe said.
If President Vaclav Havl were then unable to broker a workable government, early elections would be called. A general vote is not scheduled until the spring of 2000.

Klaus called the vote partly to spike the guns of opposition Social Democrats leader Milos Zeman who said he would propose a no-confidence vote in the government, whose popularity has slumped, at a session of parliament beginning on July 1.

"The vote of confidence, if passed, gives the government a new lease on life but it will still have to face conflicts in the coalition," Pehe said. "I do not think this government, no matter what, will ever be really stable again," he added.
